> Please specify what pre-release version you are on, many changes have happened to rendering in the 4.4 cycle

4.4.dev7

From the docs, I can't really tell what `set_content_scale_size()` is supposed to do exactly, so I can't comment on whether what you see is the expected behavior or not, but with regard to your specific use case, I feel the most straight-forward way to do this might be to just use a `Camera2D` to configure how you want your scene to be projected onto your viewport.

Assuming you want to arrange your scene at 160x200 but output it stretched to 320x200 and then have that scaled to the window according to the project settings:
- In your project settings, configure Viewport Width/Height to be 320, 200 (your output resolution before adjustments for window size)
- Set the Stretch Mode to viewport, Aspect to keep and, if you want to limit window adjustments to integral factors, Scale Mode to integer.
- In your scene, make sure the scene root is a `Node2D` (not just a `Node`, which has no transform).
- Arrange your scene content in the (0, 0) - (160, 200) area (as in your example).
- Add a `Camera2D` node, place it at (80, 100) and set its zoom to (2, 1).

If you want to also account for the 4:3 display aspect ratio, set the viewport size to 320, 240 and the `Camera2D` zoom to (2, 1.2) instead. This would produce some obvious scaling artifacts, however, because your scene pixels no longer map to the output pixels evenly. If you'd want to make these less obvious, you'd need to render at a higher resolution, for example, set the Viewport Width/Height to 1920, 1080, the Scale Mode to fractional, and the `Camera2D` zoom to (12, 5.4).

> If you want to also account for the 4:3 display aspect ratio, set the viewport size to 320, 240 and the `Camera2D` zoom to (2, 1.2) instead. This would produce some obvious scaling artifacts, however, because your scene pixels no longer map to the output pixels evenly. If you'd want to make these less obvious, you'd need to render at a higher resolution, for example, set the Viewport Width/Height to 1920, 1080, the Scale Mode to fractional, and the `Camera2D` zoom to (12, 5.4).

This is exactly the issue with doing the stretching before the viewport scaling, it needs to be performed with viewport set to stretch (to ensure pixel accuracy) but *after* the image has been upscaled to the user's screen resolution, to minimise stretching artifacts. If there's a way to manipulate the final upscaled image, this would be the point in the pipeline to double the width or set the height to 1.2, but I don't know if there is any way that's exposed in the Godot engine to allow this?

If making it easy to set a non-uniform pixel ratio isn't feasible, could it at least be possible to manipulate the final scaled image through the API?
You can do a lot of image processing along the way by using `SubViewport`s, but I don't think there's a way to access the render result after it has gone through the display scaling.

> You can do a lot of image processing along the way by using `SubViewport`s, but I don't think there's a way to access the render result after it has gone through the display scaling.

Can viewport scaling or even the upscaled render be simulated somehow? This way, the processing could be done manually instead of relying on Godot.

Yes, you can do your own viewport scaling by using either the disabled or the canvas_items Stretch Mode (depending on which coordinate system you prefer), wrapping your scene in a `SubViewport` and rendering that to a `TextureRect` via a `ViewportTexture`. I see that's what Calinou suggested in the feature request.

Getting back to the original issue: I've had a look at the source code and apparently `set_content_scale_size()` is the programmatic way to access the Viewport Width/Height setting in the project settings, i. e. your
```gdscript
get_tree().get_root().set_content_scale_size(Vector2i(320,200))
```
is supposed to have the same result as changing the project settings to a Viewport Width/Height of 320/200. And at least in your MRP that's indeed the case, so I would argue the function works as expected (if you know what to expect - I didn't) and there's no bug here.

> if you know what to expect

I think it's a prime case of "docs need improved" then

Or maybe I read that wrong, but I went back to check why I didn't understand the [documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_window.html#class-window-property-content-scale-size) the first time around:

*Base size of the content (i.e. nodes that are drawn inside the window). If non-zero, Window's content will be scaled when the window is resized to a different size.*

I found this confusing because:
- "Base size" is not mentioned in the project settings and I wasn't aware that this is a technical term that corresponds to the "Viewport Width/Height". That connection is made on the [Multiple Resolutions](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/rendering/multiple_resolutions.html#base-size) page, which doesn't explicitly state it either, but has a screenshot with a yellow box around those settings.
- I think the comment about the nodes is meant to explain what "content" is, but I read that as explaining how to determine the "base size of the content" and thought this might be something like a bounding box around the current scene.
- I thought that "when the window is resized to a different size" means "when the size of the window changes" when it actually means "when the window size is different from the base size".

So to explain to myself what actually happens here:
- The `content_scale_size` gets or sets the "base size" (Viewport Width/Height in the project settings).
- This has nothing to do with whether and where there are nodes in the current scene.
- Setting the base size to (0, 0) is the same as using `CONTENT_SCALE_MODE_DISABLED`.

And for a bit more detail:
- The specific meaning of the base size depends on the `content_scale_mode`:
    - With `CONTENT_SCALE_MODE_DISABLED`, the base size is irrelevant. Godot renders directly to the window's client area at a 1:1 scale. A node at (100, 100) will appear 100 pixels from the left and top edge of the window.
    - With `CONTENT_SCALE_MODE_CANVAS_ITEMS`, the base size defines a range of virtual coordinates that map to the window's client area. For example, a base size of (1, 1) would mean that (0, 0) is the top left of the window, (0.5, 0.5) is the center and (1, 1) is the bottom right. As with `CONTENT_SCALE_MODE_DISABLED`, the actual render resolution is determined by the window size, but there's now an internal translation between the virtual coordinate system and the actual pixel coordinates.
    - With `CONTENT_SCALE_MODE_VIEWPORT`, the base size determines the resolution of the render buffer. This buffer image is then scaled up or down to fit into the window. A node at (100, 100) will appear 100 render buffer pixels from the left and top edge of the render buffer.
- In `CONTENT_SCALE_MODE_CANVAS_ITEMS` and `CONTENT_SCALE_MODE_VIEWPORT`, "window coordinates" may refer to a subregion of the physical window if aspect correction is enabled via `content_scale_aspect` or integral scaling is enabled via `content_scale_stretch`.
- `content_scale_factor` essentially zooms in to the top left corner of the window. I suppose this is mostly useful in `CONTENT_SCALE_MODE_DISABLED` if you want "semi-virtual coordinates" that are just a scaled version of the window coordinates.
Just found content_scale_size and had to google around to find anything about it. Yeah, the documentation makes no sense.

I also find the name of the property content scaling to be confusing. The documentation is not clean as @bs-mwoerner explained. 

And it doesn't seem I am able to set the viewport to (0,0) from the editor, so is setting it to (0,0) using `get_tree().root.content_scale_size` is possible?

I think first the name of the property needs to be changed to `root_viewport_size` and also to fix the documentation since it is so vague.

> And it doesn't seem I am able to set the viewport to (0,0) from the editor, so is setting it to (0,0) using get_tree().root.content_scale_size is possible?

You can't set the Viewport's size to 0x0, as it needs a valid texture to render to (0x0 is not a valid texture size). However, you can set its content scale size to 0x0, which will make it act like the stretch mode is **Disabled** regardless of what it actually is.

@Calinou I already know that we can't set it to (0,0). And @bs-mwoerner already mentioned that setting it to (0,0) will disable stretch mode. 

But thanks for proving my point which is there are discrepancies (or ambiguity to be exact) between the setting in the Project Settings, the name of the property (content size, not root viewport size) and what it does in the documentation.

First thing, why is setting content scale size to (0,0) is allowed in the first place? This effectively changes another property which is the stretch mode, I would call this a bad software design since a user might not be aware of the side effect.

Is setting the content scale to negative numbers allowed (-500,-300)? if not (which should be), then (0,0) should not be possible since we can't do that from the editor.

Unless "content scale size" is not the same as "root viewport size" the one we find in project settings? If it is the same, then setting it to (0,0) should not be allowed, and the name of the property should be changed to something close to what it does, like `root_viewport_size`. Root since we can have subviewports and root is basically the game window here.

> First thing, why is setting content scale size to (0,0) is allowed in the first place? This effectively changes another property which is the stretch mode, I would call this a bad software design since a user might not be aware of the side effect.

It's probably a legacy holdout, but we should probably not change this to avoid breaking compatibility with existing projects which might rely on this behavior.
